chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza, from Usman al-Asbahani, who said:

I gifted a sulsul (ring-dove) to Ismail ibn Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him). So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) entered, and when he saw it, he said: 'This is the inauspicious bird. Remove it, for it is saying, "I have lost you, I have lost you." Therefore, lose it before it loses you.'

key_terms.أَخْرِجُوهُ: Remove it / Take it out (from the house or enclosure).
key_terms.صُلْصُلًا: A type of ring-dove, specifically the European turtle dove, known for its cooing call.
key_terms.فَقَدْتُكُمْ: I have lost you (plural), a pun on the bird's call and the concept of being lost/perished.

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the 'inauspicious bird' (al-sulsul) in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) identifies the 'sulsul' (a type of ring-dove) as a 'inauspicious bird' (*al-tayr al-mashum*), linking its natural cooing call to a spiritual warning. The play on words between the bird's cry ('I have lost you') and the concept of perishing (*faqidukum*) serves as a metaphor for how attachment to such creatures or their associated omens can lead to spiritual loss. This reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of interpreting natural phenomena through the lens of divine signs and practical wisdom for the believer.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from Bakr Bin Salih, from Muhammad Bin Ab Hamza, from Usman Al Asbahany who said,

‘I gifted a Sulsula to Ismail, son of Abu Abdullahasws. So Abu Abdullahasws came over, and when heasws saw it, said: ‘This is the inauspicious bird. Exit it, for it is saying, ‘You are all lost, you are all lost!’ Therefore lose it before it loses you all’.
en.sarwar: 2. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Bakr ibn Salih from Muhammad ibn abu Hamzah from ‘Uthman al-Asbahaniy who has said the following: “

I once gave a Sulsul as a gift to Tsma’il, son of abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, and abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, came in. When he (the Imam) saw it he said, ‘This bird is an unfortunate bird, so you must send it away. It says, ‘I have failed to find you, I have failed to find you.’ You must lose it before it fails to find you.”’
